image.title: Showing the boundaries of the Registrar-General's districts on the south side of the Thames in London, and also the water supply of those districts.
image.note: The small image is a pure downscale of the same plate (aspect 1.2716 against 1.2710), so both share these bounds.

model.kind: north-up affine, no rotation, independent linear scales in longitude and latitude
model.why: The compass rose on the plate is vertical, so the plate needs no rotation. The two axes were fitted separately and agreed on scale to 0.09% (aspect 1.0009), which is what a true survey-based plan produces and a sketch does not.

accuracy.note: These residuals are dominated by the identification of the control points, not by the plate. Matching an 1855 drawn feature to a modern centroid is ambiguous by tens of metres, and the independent check below agrees far more closely than the residuals do.

validation.method: Snow's plate carries a thin arc labelled 'Radius of 4 Miles from Charing Cross'. The circle of 4 statute miles about Charing Cross was projected through the fitted transform and compared with the drawn arc. This is internal to the source and independent of the control points.
validation.result: Centred on the Charles I statue (51.50736, -0.12775), the traditional datum for distances from London, the projected circle follows the drawn arc within about 5 px (16 m) at two places 2.8 km apart along it. Centred on Nominatim's 'Charing Cross' in the Strand (51.50750, -0.12369) it sits about 25 px north of the drawn arc.
validation.finding: The test validates the transform and identifies the datum: the engraver's Charing Cross is the statue, not the Strand.

limits: The transform is linear in latitude. A web map in Web Mercator stretches the image into its latitude bounds non-linearly; across the 0.11 degree height of this plate that differs by about 0.25%, a few tens of metres mid-plate.
Four control points, all of them areal features whose centroid in 1855 and today are not the same point. The accuracy figure is a measurement of this procedure, not of Snow's surveying.

No check was made of the plate's interior consistency away from the arc. A lithograph can be locally distorted by printing and by the paper, and the fold visible down the middle of the scan is not corrected for.
Nothing here establishes that features drawn on the plate are correctly placed. It establishes where the plate sits, not whether the plate is right.

attribution.controlPointCoordinates: Obtained from OpenStreetMap via the Nominatim geocoder, (c) OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL. Four point coordinates are not a substantial extract of that database, so no share-alike obligation is asserted here; the attribution is recorded because the figures came from somewhere and a reader should know where.
attribution.plate: John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 2nd ed., London: John Churchill, 1855, Map 2. Public domain. Scan via Project Gutenberg ebook 72894, from Google Books.
